AI.method: The authors replace the global minimization condition with a local one (c-approximate median) and develop a technique to explicitly construct and count the 'approximate median inverse'—the set of k-tuples of genomes for which a specific genome is a c-approximate median.
AI.result: The method allows for the calculation of the probability that a given genome is a c-approximate median and the expected number of such medians for k random genomes; it also provides upper bounds for exact medians.
AI.conclusion: The approximation is theoretically sound as approximate medians and near-optimal genomes coincide within a bounded tolerance, offering a tractable way to study genome median properties.

title: Beyond $χ^2$: Ensemble null tests for reliable scientific discovery
summary: Unrecognized systematic errors can survive standard checks and undermine scientific discoveries. Null tests and experimental controls can expose these failures, but averaging measurements or reducing them to scalar statistics can hide important structure. We propose ensemble null tests that compare multivariate distributions with references from observations or simulations. We demonstrate their benefits across science. In cosmic microwave background simulations, they detect systematic effects missed by conventional $\chi^2$ tests. In Gaia data, they detect velocity asymmetry as sensitively as an informed search. In a CRISPR screen, they expose a control mismatch in DNA damage and reveal which cellular profiles drive it. As scientific datasets grow, ensemble testing turns repeated measurements into a broader search for unknown unknowns, strengthening the empirical foundation for scientific discovery.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ensemble null tests that compare multivariate distributions to detect systematic errors that standard scalar statistics (like $\chi^2$) often miss.
AI.motivation: Standard error checks often use averaging or scalar statistics, which can mask complex systematic errors and
AI.method: Comparing multivariate distributions of experimental datasets against reference distributions from either observations or simulations.
AI.result: The method successfully detected systematic effects in cosmic microwave background simulations, velocity asymmetry in Gaia data, and control mismatches in CRISPR screens.
AI.conclusion: Ensemble null testing provides a robust framework for identifying 'unknown unknowns' in growing scientific datasets, strengthening the reliability of empirical discoveries.

title: Latent Prediction Yields Cross-Subject Alignable Representations in Sensory-Evoked fMRI
summary: Decoding sensory-evoked functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data is a central analytical tool in cognitive neuroscience. Here we ask whether self-supervised learning (SSL), which has been scarcely explored in this domain, can yield representations that support strong downstream performance. To do so, we adapt a joint embedding predictive architecture (JEPA) to train participant-specific encoders on brain data alone. The encoders never see the stimulus images or any representation derived from them. Applied to the Natural Scenes Dataset (NSD), we evaluate our learned brain embeddings on the downstream tasks of brain captioning and image reconstruction, as well as cross-participant generalization. Our self-supervised approach achieves competitive performance with parameter-rich supervised pipelines that are trained end-to-end with access to image and language data. We further find that encoders trained independently for different participants can be aligned fully unsupervised, using neither images nor stimuli shared between them. After alignment, a neural decoding head trained on one participant can be applied to another without fine-tuning and retains most of its within-subject performance on image reconstruction and brain captioning. By removing the need for images and shared stimuli, our approach is a step towards pooling fMRI data across participants and, eventually, across datasets.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a self-supervised learning (SSL) framework using a Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) to decode fMRI data without using stimulus images during training. The method achieves competitive results in brain captioning and image reconstruction and enables unsupervised cross-participant alignment, facilitating the pooling of fMRI data across subjects and datasets.
AI.motivation: Traditional fMRI decoding relies on supervised learning that requires paired stimulus (image/language) and brain data. This limits the ability to utilize unlabeled brain data and complicates data pooling across different participants or datasets.
AI.method: The researchers adapted a JEPA-based architecture to train participant-specific encoders using only brain data (unsupervised). They then applied unsupervised alignment techniques to synchronize encoders from different participants without requiring shared stimuli.
AI.result: The SSL approach performs competitively against supervised, end-to-end models. Notably, once aligned, a decoding head trained on one participant can be applied to another with minimal loss in performance, proving effective for cross-subject generalization.
AI.conclusion: This approach provides a scalable pathway for large-scale fMRI studies by allowing data to be aggregated across participants and datasets without the need for simultaneous stimulus presentation.

title: A Low-Rank Space Captures Linear Alignment Between LLM and Human Neural Activity During Naturalistic Language Listening
comment: 23 pages, 12 figures. Code: this https URL
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as computational models of human language processing, yet it remains unclear which components of their representations drive alignment with neural activity. Here, we use ridge reduced-rank regression to identify the brain-predictive subspace of LLM representations: the representational directions that support linear prediction of neural responses. Across three naturalistic language-listening datasets spanning intracranial electrophysiology and fMRI, and six model conditions spanning autoregressive, bidirectional masked, and randomly initialized language models, we find that full linear encoding performance can be recovered using only 1-3% of the original embedding dimensionality. These low-dimensional subspaces generalize across held-out participants and, to a lesser extent, across datasets, suggesting that neural predictivity is concentrated in a compact and partially shared representational space. We next compare these brain-predictive directions with the principal axes of variation in the embeddings. Principal component analysis requires substantially more dimensions to recover neural prediction, demonstrating that the directions most useful for predicting neural activity are distinct from those capturing the most overall variance within LLM representations themselves. Finally, characterizing the learned subspaces allows us to surface interpretable features that are overrepresented in neural activity above and beyond the LLM representations. Together, these results show that LLM-brain alignment is supported by a small, structured subset of model representations and provides a framework for better understanding exactly why these representations align. AI.tldr: The paper identifies a compact, low-dimensional subspace within LLM embeddings that accurately predicts neural activity (brain-predictivity), distinguishing these specific directions from the model's primary axes of variance.
AI.motivation: While LLMs align with brain activity, it is unknown which specific representational components drive this alignment and whether they overlap with the model's internal variance.
AI.method: The researchers employed **ridge reduced-rank regression** to extract a 'brain-predictive subspace' across three diverse datasets (intracranial electrophysiology and fMRI) and six model types (autoregressive, bidirectional, and random).
AI.result: • **High Efficiency:** Only 1-3% of the original embedding dimensionality is required to recover full linear encoding performance.
AI.conclusion:
• **Generalizability:** These subspaces generalize across different human participants and datasets.
• **Distinctiveness:** The brain-predictive directions are *not* the same as the Principal Components (PCA) of the LLM embeddings; the directions most useful for neural prediction are distinct from the directions of maximum variance.
• **Interpretability:** Identifying these subspaces allows researchers to isolate specific features that are overrepresented in human neural activity compared to the raw LLM output.

title: Advancing Clinical Genomic Analysis with a Skill-Centred Agent
summary: Clinical genomic analysis requires experts to integrate evolving guidelines, databases, and computational evidence. As sequencing has become increasingly accessible, this complex and labor-intensive process has become a major bottleneck to the timely use of genomic information in clinical decision-making. To fill this gap, we developed ClinGeX, a large-language-model agent that composes 105 curated executable skills through task-specific retrieval and dependency-aware orchestration. On 223 temporally held-out benchmark cases, ClinGeX achieved 71.7\% macro-averaged task-level concordance with expert reference classifications, compared with 45.7\% for the strongest comparator. In a three-condition, counterbalanced human-AI collaboration study, 45 clinical genomic professionals assessed 135 clinically derived cases under routine (no AI assistance), DeepSeek-assisted and ClinGeX-assisted conditions. ClinGeX assistance increased raw case-level concordance across criterion-level variant analysis, genomic interpretation in rare disease and molecular oncology decision-making (51.1\%, 57.8\%, 64.4\% versus 15.6\%, 31.1\%, 20.0\% in comparator conditions) and reduced reported interpretation time in all scenarios. During an exploratory one-month real-world non-interventional assessment, 11 experienced professionals submitted feedback on 96 self-selected analysis episodes and reported frequent conclusion adoption and time savings. These findings support executable domain skills as a promising approach to augment specialist genomic interpretation.

AI.tldr: ClinGeX is a large-language-model agent using 105 curated executable skills to automate clinical genomic analysis, significantly outperforming existing comparators and improving human professional performance and efficiency.
AI.motivation: The increasing accessibility of genomic sequencing has created a bottleneck in clinical decision-making because integrating evolving guidelines, databases, and computational evidence is labor-intensive and requires high expertise.
AI.method: The researchers developed ClinGeX, an LLM agent that utilizes task-specific retrieval and dependency-aware orchestration to manage 105 curated executable skills. Performance was evaluated via 223 benchmark cases and a human-AI collaboration study involving 45 professionals across three conditions (Routine, DeepSeek-assisted, and ClinGeX-assisted).
AI.result: ClinGeX achieved 71.7% macro-averaged task-level concordance (vs. 45.7% for the best comparator). In human studies, ClinGeX significantly increased concordance in variant analysis (51.1%), rare disease (57.8%), and oncology (64.4%) while reducing interpretation time. Real-world feedback confirmed frequent conclusion adoption and time savings.
AI.conclusion: The use of executable domain-specific skills within LLM agents is a promising approach to augment the efficiency and accuracy of specialist genomic interpretation in clinical settings.

title: Hyaluronic acid over-expression drives tissue architecture in both healthy and diseased states
summary: Tissue architecture is shaped by a variety of biomechanical and biochemical mechanisms, including morphogen patterning, differential growth, and spatial variations in cellular contractility. These mechanisms typically emphasize forces generated within cells. Here, we explore a complementary mechanism in which intercellular space itself exerts forces that shape tissue architecture. More specifically, we focus on hyaluronic acid (HA), a glycosaminoglycan of the extracellular matrix, that draws fluid into the spaces between cells through osmotic pressure, allowing these spaces to expand and mechanically deform the surrounding tissue. We propose that spatial patterning of HA-mediated extracellular forces, acting together with tissue geometry and junctional mechanics, provides a common physical framework capable of generating distinct tissue architectures. We test this hypothesis using a computational framework coupling a cell-based extended vertex model for biological tissues to a flow network representing HA and extracellular fluid in the extracellular space. This coupled model demonstrates a range of architectural responses spanning changes in tissue topology and morphology: global HA overexpression drives fluid accumulation and cell-cell junction rupture to produce multiple lumens in nontrivial patterns; a localized HA-rich region generates pressure gradients that drive budding; {\it multiple localized HA-rich regions generate branching;} and {\it extended HA-rich patterns can drive tubular structures.} Our results have direct experimental implications and establish the spatial patterning of HA-mediated intercellular forces as a mechanical morphogen helping shape tissue architecture.

AI.motivation: Traditional models emphasize internal cellular forces (morphogens, growth, contractility). The authors seek to understand the complementary role of the extracellular matrix (ECM) in driving mechanical deformation.
AI.method: The researchers used a computational approach combining an **extended vertex model** (for cell-based mechanics) with a **flow network model** (to represent HA and extracellular fluid dynamics).
